To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the brain regions involved in the processing of pain show age-related changes in both their structure and function, but these changes do not appear to affect the ability of older people to process pain in a clinically relevant manner.

the network of brain regions that are involved in pain processing is subject to age-related change in both structure and function, with the most pronounced changes occurring in regions of the frontal and temporal lobes, and the hippocampus.

1) Age-related decreases in brain volume occur in the prefrontl cortex and hippocampus but not brainstem structures involved in pain processing; 2) functional neuroimaging has revealed decreased pain processing in the putamen, insula, and thalamus among older adults; and 3) the functional implications of age-related changes in brain regions involved in the processing of pain are yet to fully determined.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how age-related changes in the brain affect the way that we experience pain.
the neurobiology of pain and how the brain responds to pain and the potential impact of age-related changes.
understanding the neural basis of pain and how the brain changes as we age.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
age-related changes in brain regions involved in the processing of pain are not fully understood and require further investigation.
age-related changes are likely to occur in the structure of pain processing brain regions, but the functional consequences of these changes have not been determined.
the effects of aging in pain processing are yet to be fully elucidated.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
age-related changes in the structure of the brain are not reflected in changes in the processing of pain.
the brain is not a static organ, but rather a dynamic organ that changes with age.
the aging brain has a decreased ability to process pain, and that this may contribute to the increased prevalence of chronic pain conditions in older people.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the network of brain regions that are involved in pain processing is subject to age-related change.
the network of brain regions that are implicated in the processing of pain are subject to age‐related changes in structure.
the brain regions involved in processing pain are subject to age related changes in both structure and function.
